name: Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events
title: Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events
answer: AI can help students find books they want to read, supply mentor texts that model specific writing skills, and support current events and book discussions at different reading levels. The main catch is that chatbots sometimes invent books that do not exist, so every suggestion must be checked against the school library catalog before a student goes looking for it. These uses save preparation time and keep more students in the same conversation.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea covers three ways AI supports reading and writing from kindergarten through twelfth grade. First, a student describes what they liked about a recent book, and a tool suggests titles at a similar level and topic. Second, mentor texts are short examples of the kind of writing students are learning to do, and a teacher can ask an AI tool for several model paragraphs showing a particular skill, such as a strong opening or a clear counterargument, written at different levels. Third, current events and book discussions benefit because services like Newsela offer news articles at several reading levels so a whole class can discuss the same story. The problem it solves is preparation time and keeping more students in the same conversation, while the serious catch is that chatbots sometimes invent books that do not exist.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a student describes what they liked about a recent book, and a tool suggests titles at a similar level and topic, but every suggestion is checked against the school library catalog before the student goes looking for it. For mentor texts, a teacher asks an AI tool for several model paragraphs showing a particular skill, such as a strong opening or a clear counterargument, written at different levels. Students study what makes each example work, then try the technique in their own writing, and the teacher checks the examples first and uses them as models, not as templates to copy. For current events and book discussions, a teacher can use AI to draft discussion questions for a book club, then adapt them to the group. Newsela and similar services offer news articles at several reading levels so a whole class can discuss the same story. The text gives these practices for kindergarten through twelfth grade without separating them by narrower grade bands.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this idea with a finding from researchers: chatbots sometimes invent books that do not exist, the same kind of error researchers found when a chatbot listed a teaching resource that could not be found (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). That is the only study, figure or finding the text states for this idea. The rest of the text describes practice, such as checking suggestions against the school library catalog, asking for model paragraphs at different levels, and using services that offer news articles at several reading levels. No other evidence label or research result is given.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets one serious catch at the center of this idea: chatbots sometimes invent books that do not exist, so every suggestion should be checked against the school library catalog before a student goes looking for it. For mentor texts, the teacher checks the examples first and uses them as models, not as templates to copy. For current events and book discussions, a teacher can use AI to draft discussion questions for a book club, then adapt them to the group, which keeps the teacher's judgment in the loop. The decisions that stay with a person are checking each suggested title, reviewing each model paragraph before students see it, and adapting drafted questions to the actual group. Nothing in the text removes those human checks.
